JB Pritzker visits Peach’s Restaurant in Bronzeville on Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-h/" target="_blank" >Pritzker takes personal pride in Texas Gov. Abbott’s defeat</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-k/" target="_blank" >Tina Sfondeles</a></h5><p><b>Gov's grudge</b>: Amid his reelection campaign, Gov. JB Pritzker also had Texas on his mind, having contributed $1.2 million to Democratic gubernatorial candidate <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-u/" target="_blank" >Gina Hinojosa</a> and $100,000 to U.S. Senate candidate <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-o/" target="_blank" >James Talarico</a>. Both would go on to win their races. He also contributed to several other Texas races. All of the Texas candidates Pritzker supported won Tuesday. To Pritzker, the fight to defeat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott was personal.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: In 2021, Abbott signed into law an abortion ban at six weeks of pregnancy. Pritzker then sent letters to corporate executives with ties to Texas, advising them to reconsider doing business in a state that "strips its residents of their dignity." The following year, Abbott sent thousands of migrants to Chicago. The tension boiled over in January 2024, when Pritzker pleaded with Abbott to halt migrant dropoffs in the dead of winter.</p><p><b>Boiling point</b>: Last year, Abbott took center stage in the President Donald Trump-approved battle to net Texas five additional GOP seats. Pritzker responded by taking in 40 Texas House Democrats in August 2025 to deny Republicans a quorum needed to approve the new maps. Abbott then sent Texas National Guard troops to Illinois as part of Trump's Operation Midway Blitz, although the troops were never deployed after a protracted court battle.</p><p><b>Policy playbook</b>: Declaring Democrats' electoral victories "a clear mandate" to reverse Trump's agenda, Pritzker on Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-b/" target="_blank" >laid out 200 policy proposals for his party’s new majorities to pass in Congress</a>. The agenda outlines numerous proposals to repeal broad spending cuts authorized by Trump that decimated Medicaid coverage, SNAP payments and a litany of other social services.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-n/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>HISTORIC ELECTION ✶</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c30000" name="image-c30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bb4a446/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e591746/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd727a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth applauds for U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton during a “Fighting for Illinois” press conference at the Columbus Park Refectory on the West Side to discuss the need for the next Congress to deliver urgent relief to Illinoisans. , Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd727a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c009ee5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bdd727a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fca%2F32%2F1f07296f4de295b18fcdf3f9243d%2Fday2pritzker-261105-23.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton and U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-x/" target="_blank" >Stratton’s win marks historic first for women of color in national politics</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-m/" target="_blank" >Violet Miller</a></h5><p><b>Herstory made</b>: When U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton is officially sworn in next January, Illinois will become the first state with two women of color serving in the Senate simultaneously. Stratton will also become the sixth Black woman to serve in the U.S. Senate and the second from Illinois.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: During <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-c/" target="_blank" >her victory speech Tuesday night</a>, Stratton said outgoing Sen. Dick Durbin had reminded her that the seat she was vying for is the same one Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas had once run against each other for, notably splitting on slavery. She noted her great-great-grandfather, William Stephens, was freed when the Emancipation Proclamation was signed.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-g/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>More on elections:</h4><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="line-height: inherit; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px; margin-left: 24px; padding: 0px; list-style-type: disc;" id="rte-25fa1d64-d922-11f1-ad23-45fc59ebb030"><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-q/" target="_blank" ><b>School board update</b></a>: Here's where things stand now that most races for Chicago's first-ever fully elected school board have been called.<br><b> </b></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-a/" target="_blank" ><b>Gunshot detection referendum</b></a>: More than 70% of Chicagoans expressed in an advisory referendum that they want to bring back gunshot detection technology, but the vote is unlikely to pressure Mayor Brandon Johnson into reviving it.<br><b> </b></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddkhitk-l-f/" target="_blank" ><b>GA impact</b></a>: Democrats' nationwide blue tsunami swept through Springfield on Tuesday night, too, running up the state party's supermajorities toward historic highs in the Illinois General Assembly. House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch's political operation flipped at least four districts — three additional House seats were still in play for Democrats on Wednesday.<br> </li><li><a class="Link" entries.title: Electric scooter driver dead after collision with CPD vehicle in Bridgeport
entries.summary: <p>A 39-year-old man riding an electric scooter has died after a collision with a Chicago police vehicle early Thursday in Bridgeport. </p><p>At 12:30 a.m., officers were on patrol in a marked police vehicle, traveling north on Princeton Avenue where they "came into contact" with a stand-up electric scooter operated by a 39-year-old male at 32nd Street, police said in a statement. </p><p>The scooter operator suffered injuries to his body and was taken to Stroger Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Both officers in the police vehicle were transported to a local hospital for medical treatment. </p><p>The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation by the Major Accidents Investigation Unit.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 2 teens shot in Humboldt Park alley
entries.summary: <p>Someone opened fire, hitting two boys early Thursday in a Humboldt Park alley. </p><p>The two, 15 and 17, were standing in an alley around 3 a.m. in the 1400 block of North Fairfield Avenue when they were shot, Chicago police said. </p><p>The younger boy was shot in the abdomen and taken to Stroger Hospital where he was in serious condition, police said. </p><p>The older teen was shot in the left hand and was taken to the same hospital in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>Area 5 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Losing is already taking a toll on Bulls rookie forward Caleb Wilson
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK – This is unfamiliar territory for Caleb Wilson.</p><p>And lately, it’s been a tough residency for him to live in.</p><p>Enough so that midway through the third quarter against the Knicks, Bulls coach Tiago Splitter had seen enough. Didn’t like the offense from the 20-year-old rookie, didn’t like the defense, and definitely didn’t like the body language.</p><p>So the tough-love moment resulted in Splitter sitting Wilson the rest of the game.</p><p>“You got to be more resilient,” Splitter said of the decision after Wednesday’s loss. “The game is long and I try to put myself in his shoes. Caleb probably has never been in this situation in his life. He’s always been on the winning side, winning games, and now you’ve got to be resilient even when you’re down 20, 30, 40 (points), it doesn’t matter. It’s a learning experience for sure.”</p><p>Splitter was 100% accurate on one point: Wilson has never been in this situation.</p><p>Before needing season-ending left hand surgery last year as a freshman at North Carolina, he helped lead the Tar Heels to a 19-5 record. UNC had a two-game losing streak one time.</p><p>As a senior at Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School Wilson took the program to their first-ever Georgia state championship, posting a 27-4 record and dropping a cool 33 points in the title game.</p><p>By the time Wilson & Co. play Atlanta next week, they realistically could have a 10<sup>th</sup> loss of the season in 11 games. One more loss than Wilson suffered in his previous two years of basketball combined.</p><p>Welcome to the Bulls, Rook.</p><p>“It’s never been like this for me, but I’ve just got to figure out a way through it,” Wilson admitted. “Never been through this my whole life.”</p><p>Now before outsiders start worrying that the Bulls have already broken the most talented first-year player they’ve had since Derrick Rose, take a breath. Wilson already has.</p><p>“Of course I’ve got to be resilient and help us come back from those big deficits,” Wilson said. “I have before but I just didn’t do that (Wednesday).</p><p>“It’s kind of difficult out there right now because some games it’s hard for me to get touches and things like that so I have to kind of figure out other ways to affect the game. It’s hard to catch a rhythm that way but I’ll figure it out.”</p><p>Just in case he doesn’t he also has some veteran teammates willing to help. That was the case in the locker room of Madison Square Garden after the loss, as Norman Powell was giving Wilson a few tips and reminding him to keep his head up.</p><p>“I think he takes a lot on himself, especially when we get down, you know, shouldering it and trying to do it himself,” Powell said of Wilson. “It’s all about looking within yourself and figuring out how you can get better and help impact winning.</p><p>“Being the fourth pick and coming in here, people were looking at him to kind of flip the franchise and bring some entertaining basketball. It’s a lot to shoulder but you’re going to go through it. This team has been trying to rebuild and instill a winning culture, a winning foundation, and you’re not going to do that on Day 1. You got to go through it to learn and adjust, see how we can get better.”</p><p>Competing for all four quarters is a good place for Wilson to start, but he sounded like a quick learner.</p><p>“Honestly, I feel like I should have kept playing more later in the game,” Wilson said of his early night. “I was really frustrated. Hopefully it doesn’t happen again but if it does just keep playing through it.”</p>

entries.title: Wait a sec! This isn't the Donald Trump we know.
entries.summary: <p>Words don't often fail me. I wouldn't last long in this job if they did. But Tuesday night, after sitting with a big bowl of popcorn, serenely watching the Democrats run the table in the mid-term elections — a strong majority in the House, more than enough in the Senate, even the governorship of Texas — I snapped off the television, sucked my front teeth, tweeted out a clip of Anthony Quinn doing his ecstatic Zorba the Greek dance, then went to bed.</p><p>But the <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2AzpHvLWFUM" target="_blank" >clip</a>, even without elaboration, was deceptive. I didn't feel ecstatic, or celebratory, or even particularly glad. What I felt was calm, focused, and more than a little wary. So... after all that thundering for years about rigged elections, conjuring up will-o'-the-wisps of voter fraud and mobilizing the Justice Department to chase after them, the biggest crybaby in public life since Nero is going to just shrug and go, "Oh, right, I lost. Good for you."</p><p>And we're supposed to believe him? Does that sound probable to you?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-340000" name="module-340000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Maybe I bought a bully's bluster. Didn't realize that, like the Cowardly Lion in "The Wizard of Oz," one solid bop on the nose would change him from a preening predator to a blubbering wreck, complaining that Fox News doesn't love him anymore.</p><p>Or maybe there's a Plan B — they won't certify the election. Another mob will be sicc'd on the Capitol. He tried it before.</p><p>Did he really say he was "absolutely willing" to accept the election results? That he would "look forward to working with" the Democrats? That they did a "good job"? Does that sound like the Donald Trump you've gotten to know over the past 10 years? Can I be the only one in the country who is suspicious?</p><p>Smarter political minds than my own seem to accept it. Wednesday I reached out to political wiz David Axelrod, the man who helped put Barack Obama in the White House. Why isn't Trump fighting this tooth and nail? His reply might be the most succinct remark in the history of punditry since Dorothy Parker supposedly responded to the death of Calvin Coolidge with, "How can they tell?"</p><p>"Too big to rig!" Axelrod said.</p><p>Could that be it? Yes, the scope of the loss was enormous. Seven states flipped: Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. With Mississippi — Mississippi! — incredibly, still too close to call. Governorships in Texas, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Iowa. Why not enjoy it? Grab our skis and head for hell, because obviously it's frozen over, every red state now a winter Democratic wonderland.</p><p>Why are Republicans accepting that? As I've said for years, once you get in the habit of ignoring reality, the exact nature of the reality being ignored hardly matters. The most popular and successful man on earth — in his own estimation — could just as easily use the historic rebuke as more evidence of fraud. "I'm more popular than Jesus. So obviously these results were dialed up by George Soros in a bunker in Davos, which is why I'll be imposing martial law..."</p><p>Are there facts so enormous that even Donald Trump can't ignore them? Maybe. But even if the president goes quietly — and credit to him, I suppose, for finally snapping to the value of the rule of law, if that is indeed what happened — celebration is premature. With power comes responsibility, and at 12:01 p.m. on Jan. 3, 2027 the president will start gleefully blaming every rainy day on the Democrats. He already does.</p><p>It's hard to turn a ship big as the United States. For years its been steaming toward nationalism, away from the rule of law, away from rationality, science, facts. The population has been trained to think that shutting down the government, which is supposed to help them, and giving the proceeds to rich people to make them even richer, is a good thing.</p><p>Meanwhile the Democrats often act like a herd of cats, some trying to solve every problem on earth but our own, while others want to subdivide the country into 100 identities and then focus on the smallest groups.</p><p>There's a real possibility that the wildest excesses of the Trump administration — the war on immigrants, ICE kidnapping people off the street, the FBI and the Justice Department going after the president's perceived enemies, measles being ushered back and given a cabinet post, rampant corruption and self-dealing — were shrugged off, while the public rebelled against $5-a-gallon gas. If the Democrats blow this opportunity to establish themselves as the party helping working people, those two years will snap by. Donald Trump will be 82 and eager to go after his third term. Or someone much like him. Or worse.</p>

entries.title: 'Sí, se puede' no fue solo un dicho de Dolores Huerta; ella lo vivió.
entries.summary: <p>Cuando era niño, Martin Luther King Jr. ya estaba en nuestros libros de historia. Por su parte, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/28/dolores-huerta-influential-labor-leader-feminist-and-civil-rights-icon-dies-at-96" target="_blank" >Dolores Huerta</a> se encontraba en los campos de nuestro condado.</p><p>Ella y los United Farm Workers (UFW) estaban organizando a la gente que recogía nuestros alimentos. Nuestra familia estuvo con ellos. No recuerdo haber comido uvas ni fresas durante gran parte de mi infancia. Los boicots eran la forma en que ayudábamos a los trabajadores agrícolas a luchar por sueldos justos y la dignidad que merecían. Dolores fue una de mis heroínas mucho antes de conocerla.</p><p>Más tarde, cuando llegué a ocupar cargos de liderazgo en el Movimiento por los Derechos Civiles, la conocí personalmente. Marchamos, organizamos e hicimos campaña juntos. Descubrí que era aún más extraordinaria de cerca.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-850000" name="module-850000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Hace unos años, caminaba junto al Capitolio de Estados Unidos cuando por poco no la vi. Docenas de adolescentes y universitarios de Texas estaban sentados juntos en los escalones de cemento. En medio de ellos estaba Dolores, con 92 años de edad, sentada como todos los demás. Sin silla especial. Sin alboroto. Hubieras pensado que era otra estudiante.</p><p>La llamé, sonriendo. Charlamos.</p><p>Hubo una cosa que supe no hacer. No le pregunté cómo hacía para verse tan joven. Ya había cometido ese error antes.</p><p>Estábamos haciendo campaña juntos. Ella tenía 91 años. Durante casi dos semanas había estado trabajando jornadas de 12 horas, viajando, hablando con votantes y levantándose a la mañana siguiente para repetirlo todo de nuevo.</p><p>Durante el desayuno le pregunté cómo lo hacía. Me miró y dijo, "Es fácil, Ben. Vive cada día como viviste el anterior, y nunca te detengas." Eso fue todo. Ningún secreto. Ninguna lección. Simplemente seguir adelante.</p><p>Un amigo me dijo que había visto a Dolores bailando con el rapero Common a las 2 a.m. Le creí. Claro que le creí. La última vez que la vi, Dolores tenía 94 años. Yo organizaba un evento con Jane Goodall para celebrar el 91.º cumpleaños de Jane.</p><p>Jane le preguntó al salón si había alguien allí mayor que ella. Claramente se suponía que era una pregunta retórica.</p><p>Dolores respondió que sí.</p><p>Por un momento, Jane pareció atónita. Luego reaccionó y retomó el control del salón. Tuve que reírme. Dolores había sorprendido a una de las mujeres más extraordinarias que existen simplemente siendo ella misma.</p><p>En otra ocasión, durante una comida, Dolores me contó cuánto tiempo su familia se remontaba en Nuevo México. Más de una docena de generaciones, según recuerdo. Pedí que me contara unas historias.</p><p>Bueno, había muchas. Uno de sus antepasados, dijo, pudo haber cabalgado con la banda de Gerónimo. Otro fue secuestrado por miembros de la banda cuando era niño, solo para escapar hacia un pueblo llorando, "¡Soy un cristiano!" Otro tuvo una carreta que se averió en el camino hacia el oeste. Otro fue un pastor itinerante.</p><p>Cuando terminó, estaba bastante seguro de que había abarcado a todos los personajes de todas las películas de vaqueros que había visto.</p><p>Recuerdo pensar: No es de extrañar que sea tan dura. No es de extrañar que sea tan valiente. La valentía se había transmitido en su familia por generaciones, junto con historias de cómo sobrevivir a los tiempos difíciles.</p><p>Eso también fue lo que Dolores pasó la vida haciendo por los demás. Ayudó a construir el movimiento de los trabajadores agrícolas y llevó sus lecciones a cada nueva generación. Luchó por los campesinos, por los inmigrantes, por las mujeres, por el derecho al voto.</p><p>"Sí, se puede" no era solo algo que decía. Era la manera en que vivía.</p><p>Cuando Dolores murió a los 96 años, volví a pensar en esos jóvenes texanos en los escalones del Capitolio. Estaban sentados junto a alguien que había ayudado a cambiar el mundo de sus abuelos. Ella estaba sentada entre ellos como si perteneciera allí. Y así era.</p><p>Dolores entendía algo que todo movimiento debe aprender. No le entregas el trabajo a la siguiente generación desde la distancia. Te sientas con ellos. Escuchas. Estás presente.</p><p>Extrañaré su risa, sus historias y la maravillosa sorpresa de encontrarla dondequiera que la gente se organizara. Pero seguiré oyendo su voz en el desayuno. Vive cada día como viviste el anterior. Y no te detengas.</p><p>Ahora nos toca a nosotros.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous es profesor en práctica en la Universidad de Pensilvania y ex presidente y director ejecutivo de la NAACP </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Soul Train Awards roll into Chicago with Queen Latifah
entries.summary: <p>Chicago prepared for the homecoming of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/27/soul-train-awards-chicago-november-chaka-khan-bet" >Soul Train Awards</a> with a lot of style and star power, hosting both a vibrant dance party and a special event with Queen Latifah on Wednesday.</p><p>The official ceremony will be taped tonight at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance and broadcast Nov. 27 on BET and CBS at 7 p.m.</p><p>But the festivities kicked off yesterday afternoon with the free “Soul in the City” event at the Chicago Cultural Center. entries.title: Illinois House Speaker Chris Welch faces mutiny of 26 Democrats calling for new leader after Benton scandal
entries.summary: <p>Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch’s tenure as leader of his chamber’s supermajority caucus is in jeopardy after 26 Democratic state representatives issued a statement calling for new leadership.</p><p>The mutiny comes in the wake of revelations over the summer that Welch was aware of sexual harassment allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield, almost three years before additional complaints prompted Benton’s resignation.</p><p>The letter was distributed late Wednesday by North Side state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>the most vocal public critic</u></a> of Welch’s handling of the case and his formation of a working group that she dismissed as “lip service” to addressing Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment.</p><p>But the letter drew signatures from nearly a third of the caucus that’ll be sworn in with a new General Assembly in January, including Cicero state Rep. Lisa Hernandez, chair of the Democratic Party of Illinois.</p><p>Their brief statement doesn’t name Welch or identify specific reasons for his ouster.</p><p>“Over the course of the last few months, we have grown increasingly convinced that the House Democratic Caucus needs new leadership,” the letter says. “We represent a broad spectrum of our caucus, and each have come to this decision for our own reasons. We look forward to a robust race for a new Speaker of the House.”</p><p>A Welch spokesperson didn’t have any immediate comment.</p><p>The revolt follows a historic flexing of political muscle by the three-term speaker’s political operation, which expanded Democrats’ control of the House to a modern-record 78-40 supermajority in 2022.</p><p>The Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House political committee raised $35 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/04/blue-tsunami-democrats-massive-advantage-illinois-general-assembly" target="_blank" ><u>to flip at least five more seats in Tuesday’s general election</u></a>, turning Illinois’ heavily gerrymandered political map an even deeper shade of blue. With two other seats still in play as mail ballots trickled in, that disparity could rise as high as 85-33 over Republicans.</p><p>“This is what a winning political operation looks like," Welch said in a statement issued several hours before the bloc of his colleagues called for a new speaker.</p><p>The list includes three incoming representatives freshly elected with Welch’s backing, including state Rep.-elect Jessica Dixon Heitman, who won a full term to Benton’s former seat with the help of $1.6 million in support from Welch-controlled funds.</p><p>Nineteen of the 26 signatories are women. Four are part of Welch’s own leadership team: Hernandez, who’s deputy majority leader; plus assistant majority leaders Eva-Dina Delgado, Bob Morgan and Katie Stuart.</p><p>Their votes would be enough to block Welch from the gavel even with their party’s staggering new majority.</p><p>Welch would need support from across the aisle to secure the simple 60-vote majority required to lead the chamber for a fourth term.</p><p>"For me, the decision came down to believing women who come forward as survivors of sexual harassment and creating a safer workplace environment for all who work in our Capitol and look to the Speaker for guidance and mentorship," state Rep. Anne Stava, D-Downers Grove, said in a statement. "I look forward to a robust process of selecting our new speaker of Illinois House. Change is rarely easy, but in my experience worth the sacrifices needed to get there."</p><p>Welch was elected as Illinois’ first Black speaker in 2021 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/13/22228758/emanuel-chris-welch-illinois-house-speaker-vote-mike-madigan" target="_blank" ><u>in the wake of Michael Madigan’s downfall</u></a>, which was precipitated in part by the legendary ex-political boss’ mishandling of misconduct allegations within his once-vaunted 13th Ward organization.</p><p>After Madigan’s 36 years as speaker, legislators set a limit of five terms with the gavel.</p><p>The Benton investigation raised questions about Welch’s own behavior, including social media interactions with a complainant in the Benton case that left the young woman uncomfortable, while using an encrypted messaging app to invite her to meet at a bar.</p><p>The fiasco also renewed scrutiny of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/28/illinois-house-speaker-emanuel-chris-welch-harry-benton-michael-j-madigan-sexual-harassment-inquiry" target="_blank" ><u>a 2002 suburban police report</u></a> that alleged Welch slammed a woman’s head into a countertop during an argument. He was never criminally charged and has denied wrongdoing.</p><p>But even before the Benton scandal, some House Democrats had privately grumbled about Welch’s command of sometimes chaotic caucus meetings, as well as a policy of not calling bills for a floor vote without 60 Democrats first signaling support.</p><p>Welch apologized for how he handled the case over the summer, maintaining that he had no choice but to continue backing Benton without a formal complaint to spur an investigation.</p><p>Several members passed on participating in the House working group Welch convened to discuss harassment reporting mechanisms in the Capitol.</p><p>Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Springfield Nov. 17 for the fall veto session.</p>

entries.title: Woman shot in Brighton Park road-rage attack last month dies, police say
entries.summary: <p>A 32-year-old woman shot last month in Brighton Park in what an alderperson described as a being sparked by road rage has died Thursday morning, police say. </p><p>Rosa D. Hernandez Rivera, 32 and of Brighton Park, was pronounced dead at 5:17 a.m., according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Hernandez Rivera of was a passenger in a vehicle in the 2400 block of West 47th Street about 9:30 a.m. Oct. 22, when a gray car pulled up beside her and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/22/32-year-old-woman-critical-condition-brighton-park-shooting" target="_blank" >someone shot her in her head,</a> police said. </p><p>After the shooting, the gray car sped away south on Western Avenue and Hernandez Rivera was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, initially in critical condition. </p><p>Hernandez Rivera's husband and two of their three children were also in the car, 15th Ward Ald. Raymond Lopez told the Chicago Sun-Times at the time.</p><p>Hernandez Rivera's husband had been working with police to identify public and private surveillance cameras in the area that might have captured the incident, said Lopez at the time, who added that he believes road rage sparked the shooting.</p><p>No one else was hurt.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: As several other major cities boost arts funding, Chicago’s proposed 2027 cultural spending plan is flat
entries.summary: <p>Funding for the department that puts on Chicago’s large-scale events, such as Jazz Festival and Taste of Chicago, would remain essentially flat under Mayor Brandon Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/20/mayor-brandon-johnson-failed-corporate-head-tax-resurrected-proposed-budget" target="_blank" ><u>proposed 2027 budget</u></a>.</p><p>The Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events is set to receive about $62.5 million next year in the proposed budget. That’s up less than 1% from the arts budget that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/city-hall/2025/11/05/chicago-dcase-cultural-affairs-budget-clinee-hedspeth-kenya-merritt-grants-arts" target="_blank" ><u>passed City Council last year</u></a>.</p><p>At a budget hearing Wednesday at City Hall, commissioner <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/12/16/chicago-cultural-department-dcase-grants-kenya-merritt-chief-mayor-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>Kenya Merritt</u></a> said the department’s “commitment to Chicago's creative community remains unwavering.”</p><p>“Arts and culture are essential to our city's identity, economic vitality, as well as our quality of life,” Merritt told City Council.</p><p>But amid a broader budget shortfall, aldermen spent much of Wednesday’s hearing asking Merritt about the rollout of an initiative that would do more to recover funds the city spends to support special events, ranging from <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/04/18/chicago-street-festivals-costs-security-pride-wicker-park-randolph" target="_blank" ><u>neighborhood street fests</u></a> to large-scale music festivals.</p><p>Recouping the cost of city services allocated to such events, like police and sanitation, was among cost-cutting and revenue-raising ideas outlined in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/obm/supp_info/2026Budget/Financial%20and%20Strategic%20Reform%20Options%20-%20City%20of%20Chicago.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>2025 report</u></a> from the consulting group EY. Merritt said implementation is still in the works and what the changes will look like for event organizers is not yet clear.</p><p>“We have to strike a balance,” Merritt said. “We don't want to be in a position where we're losing events. They're so critical to our economy as well as to our neighborhoods.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Private foundations that buttress the arts have also shifted their priorities elsewhere.</p><p>In September, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/03/chicago-arts-funding-mayor-brandon-johnson-city-budget-cuts" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times reported</u></a> that New York, Los Angeles, Houston and Phoenix all increased funding to their city’s cultural departments by at least 2% in their most recent budgets. In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani allocated a <a class="Link" href="https://www.artforum.com/news/mamdani-allocates-a-record-323-million-for-culture-1234753986/" target="_blank" ><u>record-setting $323.8 million</u></a> for the local cultural department, an 8% increase from the year before.</p><p>Johnson told WBEZ/Sun-Times at the time, “My commitment will be consistent, and I’ll remain vigilant in my call to invest more in the arts.” The mayor added that, “Making the investments in arts and culture, that I believe is the way to define my administration.”</p><p>In addition to special events, DCASE also includes the city’s film office and provides funding directly to artists and arts organizations across Chicago. Merritt said Wednesday the department remains committed to grantmaking, despite the department having spent down the last of federal COVID-relief dollars, which helped to boost those In addition to special events, DCASE also includes the city’s film office and provides funding directly to artists and arts organizations across Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Timothy Hiatt/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 2025, DCASE awarded a total of $10.8 million in grants to artists and arts organizations across several programs, according to public records. Instead, funding remained the same.</p><p>“We're disappointed,” said Claire Rice, the group’s executive director. “We would have loved to see, especially after the remarks by the mayor underscoring his support for the arts, for that to correspond to support in the DCASE budget.”</p><p>Rice also pointed to the study the alliance released this summer that found the cultural sector is Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/06/25/creative-economy-impact-study-arts-alliance-illinois-workers" target="_blank" ><u>third-largest workforce</u></a>. “We're really an investment strategy,” Rice said. “It's not a charitable donation. This year, in a change from that model, DCASE is set to receive a small amount ($133,580) from the city’s corporate fund for salaries for the two new proposed positions.</p><p>The Better Government Association notes it's the first time the cultural department has received corporate fund dollars since 2011, under former Mayor Richard M. Daley. According to a DCASE spokesperson, the new positions will be focused on special events cost recovery and that those costs recovered would reimburse the corporate fund.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i><br></p>

entries.title: Downtown 'Cultural Stadium' idea picks up steam with new leadership, $2 million funding
entries.summary: <p>A long-discussed vision to revitalize <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/downtown" target="_blank" ><u>Downtown</u></a> Chicago as an arts-filled “Cultural Stadium” is now in motion, with the appointment announced this week of a leader to helm the project.</p><p>Former Michigan state representative Donna Lasinski was announced Wednesday as the initiative’s inaugural president. Under her leadership, the Cultural Stadium plans to build on Chicago’s already-vibrant arts scene and “transform existing infrastructure and underused public spaces into new cultural experiences,” according to a press release from the group.</p><p>Backed by $2 million in private, corporate and government funds, the idea for the so-called <a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/" target="_blank" ><u>“Cultural Stadium”</u></a> was created by Lou Raizin, the president and CEO of Broadway In Chicago. The proposal aims to weave arts and culture into the everyday lives of Chicagoans, especially those working in or visiting the Loop.</p><p>The six-figure gift came from cultural leaders Abby O'Neil, a founding board member of the Harris Theater and Carroll Joynes, a co-founder of the University of Chicago’s Cultural Policy Center.</p><p>The project has been discussed in abstract for years but is now moving from idea to reality with the appointment of Lasinski, who has served as the Cultural Stadium’s senior adviser since April. Lasinski has an extensive background in politics, education and public service; according to her LinkedIn, she served as a trustee on the school board of Ann Arbor Public Schools from 2014 to 2016 and founded education company ThinkStretch, LLC in 2008.</p><p>Some programming has already been piloted this summer and fall. Through a Cultural Umbrella pilot program that offered free days for children and their families to access the city’s major cultural institutions, more than 400 children and their parents attended events at places such as The Joffrey Ballet, Chicago History Museum, Chicago Children's Theatre and the Adler Planetarium. The effort was funded by a $50,000 grant from the Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events.</p><p>Also underway is “Poetry Way,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/dance/2026/09/03/greg-cameron-joffrey-ballet-ceo-to-step-down-2027-arts-financial-turnaround" target="_blank" ><u>the creation of a digital display</u></a> in the alleyway between Joffrey Tower and the Chicago Theatre in the Loop. The collaboration between the Poetry Foundation and the Joffrey Ballet launched during the Chicago Loop Alliance Arts Fest in October. A permanent debut is set for March 2027.</p><p>More downtown alleyways could be transformed under the Cultural Stadium. The website calls the project “Midblock” and aims to turn “overlooked alleys and service corridors” into vibrant and bustling gathering places.</p><p>The first of the murals features a giant koi pond by local artist <a class="Link" href="https://ryantovakatz.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Ryan Tova Katz</u></a> on the roof of the parking garage at 181 N. Clark St.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0f0000" name="image-0f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e3e6bf3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b8d7cf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f64f92b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A mural by Ryan Tova Katz atop the parking garage at 181 N. Clark St., commissioned by the Cultural Stadium" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f64f92b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d5ab5f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f64f92b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/542x304+0+169/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0c%2F7a%2F597e055249a98c0024d72966769e%2Fimage-4.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p class="cms-textAlign-left">A mural by Ryan Tova Katz atop the parking garage at 181 N. Clark St., commissioned by the Cultural Stadium</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Douglas Jubic/Cultural Stadium</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>According to the Cultural Stadium website, other potential projects include <a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/vision/thelink" target="_blank" ><u>“The Link,”</u></a> which proposes turning a portion of Lower Wacker Drive into a music venue; <a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/vision/vault" target="_blank" ><u>“The Vault,”</u></a> a large canopy and pedestrian walkway imagined for LaSalle Street, between Jackson Blvd. and Adams St.; and <a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/vision/thepause" target="_blank" ><u>“The Pause,”</u></a> which aims to “transform the humble public restroom into a bold statement of what a great city can be.”</p><p>Chicago has recently taken steps to<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/03/chicago-self-cleaning-toilet-what-to-know" target="_blank" ><u> install its first public restroom</u></a> in West Town.</p><p>Though many details were not available, the Cultural Stadium plan also envisions transforming vacant retail and office spaces in Downtown Chicago into affordable studios for working artists and a year-long residency program that would allow creatives to live rent-free, called <a class="Link" href="https://www.culturalstadium.com/vision/thecommunity" target="_blank" ><u>“The Community.”</u></a></p>

entries.title: Muere conductor de patín eléctrico en Bridgeport tras choque con vehículo de la Policía de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre de 39 años que conducía un patín eléctrico murió tras chocar con un vehículo de la Policía de Chicago a primeras horas del jueves en Bridgeport.</p><p>A las 12:30 a.m., los agentes patrullaban en un vehículo policial marcado, circulando hacia el norte por Princeton Avenue, cuando "entraron en contacto" con un scooter eléctrico operado por un hombre de 39 años en la calle 32th, dijo la policía en un comunicado.</p><p>Mientras se desarrollaba la situación, un agente de la policía en la escena le suplicó a una operadora del 911, preguntando cuándo llegaría la ayuda médica.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>"Necesitan llegar lo antes posible", le dijo el agente a la operadora.</p><p>"De nuevo sin ETA (hora estimada de llegada)", respondió.</p><p>"Está bien, tenemos un hombre hispano, de 25 a 35 años, heridas masivas en la cabeza, mucha pérdida de sangre en este momento", dijo el agente.</p><p>El conductor del patín sufrió lesiones en el cuerpo y fue trasladado a Stroger Hospital, donde fue declarado muerto, dijo la policía.</p><p>Ambos agentes que iban en el vehículo policial fueron trasladados a un hospital local para recibir atención médica.</p><p>Las circunstancias que rodean el incidente permanecen bajo investigación por la Unidad de Investigación de Accidentes Mayores.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears report: LT Theo Benedet back at practice
entries.summary: <p>What happened Thursday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Theo back</h3><p>Starting left tackle Theo Benedet practiced Thursday, one day after being listed as out on the Bears' estimated injury report because of a shoulder injury suffered Monday night. He was limited in practice, though. The Bears would start Ozzy Trapilo in his place were he unable to play Sunday against the Buccaneers.</p><p>"I think being able to rotate Ozzy in has been great for him to kind of build back up to what a potential load could be in terms of starting, playing more than he has," offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. "I feel pretty good about the path we've put him on to be able to do that if needed.”</p><p>Defensive tackle Grady Jarrett was upgraded to limited, too, after sitting out Wednesday with a groin injury. Malik Muhammad, who missed Monday's game with a toe injury, was limited, too.</p><h3>Monangai still out</h3><p>The Bears aren't likely to get running back Kyle Monangai back until after the team's bye next week. He didn't practice Thursday while he continues to tend to the toe he hurt in Week 3. Linebacker D'Marco Jackson sat out with an ankle problem, while guard Joe Thuney got his standard veteran day off.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Now that the Valkyries are champions, is Veronica Burton the point guard to beat?
entries.summary: <p>After the Valkyries took a 3-2 lead in the WNBA Finals, coach Natalie Nakase called Veronica Burton the best point guard in the league.</p><p>Given that the Valkyries went on to win the championship, Nakase had earned some bragging rights.</p><p>And her point guard absolutely came through, hitting huge shots and steadying her team through a marathon Finals.</p><p>Still, giving Burton the crown made me think about the players who might take offense to it, like first-team All-WNBA guards Caitlin Clark and Olivia Miles.</p><p>Though their teams lost in the first round of the playoffs, they seem to represent the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba/2026/07/24/is-caitlin-clark-the-best-point-guard-at-all-star-weekend-relax-shes-definitely-one-of-them" >future of the superstar point guard</a>, one that can lead the team in scoring in addition to setting up their teammates.</p><p>Burton is a very different kind of player.</p><p>Her numbers aren’t usually gaudy — she averaged nine points, 5.7 rebounds and 3.7 assists in the Finals. But she’s always been one of the best defenders in the country. As a junior at Northwestern, she became the only player to hold Clark to fewer than 10 points in her college career.</p><p>Plus, her offensive strengths feed directly into what the Valkyries want to do, which is to limit turnovers and create second-chance opportunities.</p><p>Burton averaged only 1.5 turnovers during the Finals and is also the best offensive rebounder at her position. That helped the Valkyries win the possession battle, which was a deciding factor in their success.</p><p>Heading into the 2027 season, I’ll be watching to see whether this remains a Valkyries specialty or becomes a defining league trend. If winning the possession battle becomes a must, what does it mean for the championship aspirations of a turnover-prone player like Clark?</p><p>When Clark entered the league, I bought into the idea that her turnovers fit neatly into the model of her greatness. Sometimes her passes might fly over her teammates’ heads, but that’s the price of playing at such a fast pace.</p><p>I remember when Christie Sides, the Fever coach during Clark’s rookie season, said she wanted Clark to average fewer than two turnovers per game, I thought: fat chance. Clark would always turn it over more than that, and that was OK.</p><p>I’m not so sure about that anymore — both the notion that she can’t take better care of the ball, and that it will be okay if she doesn’t.</p><p>I think the Valkyries and the runner-up Dream, both likely to be juggernauts for years to come, are too good at making teams pay for their turnovers. And I don’t think Clark’s turnovers are totally a product of her pace.</p><p>In the Fever’s Game 3 loss to the Aces, for example, most of her giveaways came from ballhandling errors and careless passes in the half court. A player with Clark’s IQ should be able to fix that.</p><p>She already sees the game better than most of her peers. It’s part of why the Fever recorded the best offensive numbers in the history of the league this past season. She regularly has stretches of perfection, making the right read on every play.</p><p>Then, suddenly, without the defense really changing anything, she starts throwing it away. Those are the mental lapses that need fixing.</p><p>So in the wake of the Valkyries' success, my new outlook on Clark is this: to become a championship point guard, I think she will have to maintain her pace while also bringing her turnovers closer to Sides’s old target.</p><p>For now though, Burton and Nakase should enjoy their crowns.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: CATCH-22: Bears TE Sam Roush hoping to make a world of difference
entries.summary: <p>Analyzing the Bears with the help of 22 names, starting with …</p><p><b>Sam Roush (1), </b>the rookie tight end who played a whopping 53% of the Bears’ snaps Monday in place of <b>Cole Kmet (2)</b>. The third-round rookie has just three catches this year for 33 yards this year.</p><p>“He's done a good job with what we've asked him to do ...” offensive coordinator <b>Press Taylor (3)</b> said. “We have a lot of mouths to feed.”</p><p>Roush spent ages 9-12 halfway across the world. His father’s business took their family to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, for six months and then Jakarta, Indonesia, for about three years.</p><p>Roush kept himself entertained by chasing bugs and lizards outside his home.</p><p>“Like any 10-year old boy,” he said, “that was kinda my thing.”</p><p>He can still detail his favorite finds: a lizard that expanded its arms to glide and a tailless whip scorpion that he later saw in a “<b>Harry Potter” (4)</b> movie. He had to be careful to avoid venomous snakes.</p><p>“You don’t wanna go wandering into a grassy field,” he said.</p><p>Roush has made his living running in one. At first, though, he played rugby in southeast Asia. When he returned home, he realized he didn’t know the same rock bands his American friends did.</p><p><b>“</b>I missed out on a couple years of culture,” he said. “I was a little bit of a weird kid.”</p><p><b>Trent Dilfer (5), </b>the former NFL quarterback and ESPN personality who coached Roush at Lipscomb Academy, uses a different descriptor.</p><p>“He’s just different than 99 percent of the kids his age,” Dilfer told me. “He’s more cultured, more mature and, I think, tougher … mentally and physically.”</p><p>When he moved to Nashville before his senior high school season, Roush had already committed to play for <b>David Shaw (6) </b>— he was Stanford’s second-ranked recruit, behind future No. 2 overall pick <b>David Bailey (7)</b>. Dilfer convinced him to play defensive line to improve his physicality and was delighted by his “lack of entitlement.”</p><p>He’s comfortable in his own skin, too, something Roush attributes that to moving seven times — from coast-to-coast and overseas — before attending college. He can be goofy. He wore glasses with tape on the bridge for his senior mug shot, a Stanford tight end tradition.</p><p>“Stanford men are comfortable with the rigors of life,” Dilfer said. “And free spirits.”</p><h3><b>Roush’s best advice has come from …</b></h3><p><b>Phil Olsen</b> <b>(8)</b>, his maternal grandfather, who was drafted fourth overall in 1970 and played six NFL seasons. When Roush made mistakes earlier this season — he dropped a touchdown and whiffed on a blocked field goal in the final minutes of the Bears’ Week 2 loss to the Vikings, and botched punt coverage in Week 3 — his grandfather told him to take the outside pressure in stride.</p><p>“Obviously it’s more than it was in college,” Roush said, “but it really shouldn’t impact my process at all.”</p><p>Roush bought a Brick, a device that limits screen time on his phone. That helped.</p><p>“I just locked all my social media,” he said.</p><p>Football runs in Roush’s family. Phil’s brother <b>Merlin</b> <b>(9)</b> went to 14 Pro Bowls and later starred in “Little House on the Prairie” and on NFL and college football broadcasts. Phil’s other brother <b>Orrin</b> <b>(10)</b> played for the Chiefs.</p><p>Roush’s dad <b>Luke (11)</b> played defensive back at Duke. <b>John Roush</b> <b>(12)</b>, Sam’s paternal grandfather, played running back at Ohio, while uncle <b>Mark Roush (13)</b> played safety at Northwestern. He has family members who have played linebacker at Stanford and defensive tackle at BYU, too.</p><h3><b>Playing 14% of the tight end snaps Monday was …</b></h3><p><b>Stephen Carlson (14), </b>who was promoted from the practice squad as part of the league’s one-day-only standard elevation program. On Wednesday, he was put on the 53-man roster for just the second time in his four years with the Bears. The first time it happened, in 2024, he broke his collarbone in practice two days later and never made it to Sunday.</p><p>Looking back, Carlson said, it’s remarkable how healthy the tight ends have been since he joined the Bears’ practice squad in 2023. Carlson, who turns 30 next month, has played in only four games for the Bears.</p><p>“I’ve been working hard the past couple years and patiently waiting,” he said.</p><p>Kmet once joked the tight end room “displays as a smarter room than it actually is,” given that he went to Notre Dame, Roush to Stanford and <b>Colston Loveland (15)</b> to Michigan. Tight ends coach <b>Jim Dray</b> <b>(16)</b> is a Stanford alum, while practice-squadder <b>Qadir Ismail (17)</b> — son of <b>Qadry “The Missile” Ismail (18)</b> and nephew of <b>Raghib “Rocket” Ismail (19), </b>both college stars — went to Villanova and Samford.</p><p>Carlson might have them all beat — he played wide receiver at Princeton. He’s from small Jamestown, N.Y. — as was <b>Lucille Ball (20) — </b>which is so far west that a drive to Chicago is roughly as the same distance as one to the Hamptons. He said he had “no expectations” of a pro career — through his first two Princeton seasons, he caught two passes.</p><p>Carlson was convinced by his agent to add 20 pounds between the end of his senior year and his pro day and try out as a tight end. Former Bear <b>Jesper Horsted (21), </b>his fellow Princeton receiver, made the same switch at the same time.</p><p>Carlson majored in Ecology and Evolution Biology. One summer, he’d work out at dawn and spend the rest of the morning shirtless and on a kayak in Carnegie Lake near campus, dropping probes in the water to measure oxygen levels.</p><p>“Econ majors and political science majors are doing anything like that,” he said with a smile.</p><h3><b>An honorary tight end — and genuine CFL fan — is …</b></h3><p><b>Tackle Theo Benedet (22)</b>, who was used as an extra blocker 13 times last year. He grew up in Vancouver, Canada, but wasn’t a Seahawks fan.</p><p>He liked the Lions.</p><p>Detroit, really?</p><p>“BC,” he said.<br></p>

entries.title: LIV Golf will shut down after a five-year run
entries.summary: <p>TRENTON, N.J. — LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn't have enough support.</p><p>"The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan," attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. "Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business."</p><p>LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.</p><p>It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable "LIV 2.0." But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren't interested.</p><p>"BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement. "While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."</p><p>Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.</p><p>Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players' last LIV appearance.</p><p>LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O'Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn't going forward.</p><p>LIV suffered two big setbacks, before and after filing for bankruptcy.</p><p>The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the DP World Tour in Europe.</p><p>Then, DP World Tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.</p><p>Kinnings said in an interview with The Scotsman newspaper earlier this week, "But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to 'destroy the DP World Tour.'"</p><p>But the biggest setback was in April, two weeks after the Masters and two months after the start of the Iran war. PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.</p><p>LIV was originally run by Greg Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as "Golf, but louder" with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.</p><p>But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.</p><p>The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.</p><p>Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.</p><p>LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV's final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European tour Q-school last week.<br></p>

entries.title: UI Health providers authorize strike amid dispute over pay raises
entries.summary: <p>Hundreds of UI Health's advanced practice nurses, physician assistants and midwives voted to strike last week after they say they were denied raises given to other hospital workers.</p><p>The 200 providers voted "overwhelmingly" to deliver a 10-day strike notice on Friday to the Illinois Educational Labor Relations Board and University of Illinois Chicago, according to their union, SEIU Local 73. The union says UIC denied the providers a 2% wage increase in August that was given to other hospital staff.</p><p>The providers could strike as soon as Nov. 11. The union, which has not announced if and when they'll strike, says they would rather negotiate than strike. But SEIU and UIC have been at odds for over a year over whether the union is allowed to represent the providers, and UI Health says the strike would violate a court order. </p><p>“UIC Advanced Practice Providers have voted to strike because of the egregious behavior of their employer, which refuses to come to the bargaining table and continues their lawsuit to stop the workers from gaining the respect and compensation they deserve," SEIU Local 73 President Dian Palmer said in a news release.</p><p>SEIU Local 73 also claims UIC filed a motion with the state appellate court to stop bargaining while also saying that any wage increase would need to be bargained. </p><p>"This duplicitous behavior is what led to workers voting to strike," the union said in a statement. SEIU says the 200 providers have gone two years without a raise or a cost-of-living adjustment. </p><p>In a statement, UI Health says the state appellate court entered an order temporarily pausing collective bargaining between the university and the union. </p><p>"UI Health maintains that a strike would be unlawful while the court's order remains in effect and until the legal requirements for a lawful strike have been met. We expect the union to follow the law and allow the legal process to proceed," the statement reads. "Should a work stoppage occur, we have comprehensive contingency plans in place to maintain operations and ensure safe, high-quality patient care at the University of Illinois Hospital & Clinics."</p><p>The providers are also "fighting for pay that keeps pace with the market, pay transparency and equity, safe staffing, and the ability to take meal breaks and use earned sick time," according to their union. </p>

entries.title: White Sox officially announce hire of amateur scouting director Matt Roffe
entries.summary: <p>The biggest hire for the White Sox offseason up to this point is now official. He just had to take part in the Milwaukee Brewers’ World Series victory parade first.</p><p><b>Matt Roffe</b> (pronounced “ROW-fay”) has been named the club’s new director of amateur scouting; replacing <b>Mike Shirley</b> after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>he resigned in September</u></a>. News of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>Roffe’s hire broke last week</u></a>, a day after his previous employer defeated the Rays.</p><p>The Sox stuck with the traditional title for the man tasked with running their drafts going forward. But the hire of a 30-year-old who most recently served as an assistant director of domestic scouting for the famously progressive Brewers fit general manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/14/white-sox-could-reimagine-amateur-scouting-process-in-the-wake-of-mike-shirleys-resignation-chris-getz-luis-castillo-edgar-quero-mike-shirley-mlb-draft" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chris Getz</u></b><u>’s comments in September</u></a> about reimagining their draft process. Industry sources that spoke to the Sun-Times praised Roffe for his creativity and willingness to explore new routes for uncovering talent.</p><p>“It’s just empowering scouts and giving them a voice, and trying to blend the objective information that’s in place with their subjective take on players,” Roffe said of the process he’ll bring over from Milwaukee. “The opportunity to combine all those different inputs into a single valuation is really exciting.”</p><p>On top of being younger than left-hander <b>Anthony Kay</b>, Roffe’s rise in the amateur scouting ranks really encompasses his last five years in Milwaukee, as he impressed on the professional scouting side of the business with the Diamondbacks for the two seasons prior, with a pair of internship years with the Padres and Brewers–and even some time working for MLB’s Statcast–before that. The Brewers hiring Roffe back away from the Diamondbacks was viewed as a statement on the strength of his work as their intern.</p><p>“That just gave me a good foundation for what to look for so when I came to the Brewers and started spending more time in the draft, I really had a good foundation of the types of things that translate to value in the big leagues,” Roffe said of his prior experience. “The interview process [with the White Sox], it was very thorough. It was just an enjoyable process to go through, and I felt like the organization has made great strides over the last two years.”</p><p><b>Marsh added to pitching depth</b></p><p>It’s not quite the offseason hot stove firing at maximum capacity, but the White Sox also announced the signing of 28-year-old right-hander <b>Alec Marsh</b> to a minor league deal with an invite to spring training.</p><p>A former Royals’ second-round pick, Marsh’s last major-league action came in Kansas City in 2024, where he covered 129 innings in 26 appearances (25 starts) with a 4.53 ERA. Marsh touts roughly average velocity while his breaking stuff earns the plaudits, but has been sidelined by shoulder impingement the past two years, before he was outrighted by the Royals and elected free agency in October.</p><p>Marsh’s Royals tenure gives him past work experience with White Sox pitching <b>Zach Bove</b>.</p><p><b>Silver Slugger finalists</b></p><p>The White Sox offense led the American League in runs scored this past season, and the fallout will extend beyond <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/04/white-sox-assistant-hitting-coach-joel-mckeithan-departing-for-promotion-with-cardinals" target="_blank" ><u>their assistant hitting coach getting hired away by the Cardinals.</u></a></p><p><b>Chase Meidroth</b> (second base), <b>Miguel Vargas</b> (third base), <b>Tristan Peters</b> (outfield) and <b>Sam Antonacci</b> (utility player) have all been named finalists for Silver Slugger awards at their respective positions. Additionally, the Sox are one of four finalists for a team Silver Slugger award.</p>

entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 9 vs. Buccaneers
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> experts make their picks for "Sunday Night Football" against the Buccaneers at Soldier Field:</p><h3><b>Patrick Finley</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 23-20: </b>The last time the Bears beat the Buccaneers, in 2020, Tom Brady defeated Nick Foles in a rematch of the "Philly Special" Super Bowl. <b>Season</b>: 3-5.</p><h3><b>Jason Lieser</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 27-21:</b> This one seems like it should be lopsided in the Bears' favor, but nothing is ever as easy as it looks in the NFL, and primetime games in particular tend to be tight. <b>Season:</b> 4-4.</p><h3><b>Scoop Jackson</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Bears, 42-20:</b> They’ve been anointed. After Monday night’s performance they became <i>that</i> team. Front-runners. If there ever was a trap game for an NFL team this season, this game is it. The Bears won’t be trapped. <b>Season</b>: 4-4.</p><h3><b>Steve Greenberg</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 27-16:</b> After a short week of prep, the performance might not check all the boxes. Super Bowl contender problems, right? Can't go against the Bears now. <b>Season</b>: 5-3.</p><h3><b>Jeff Agrest</b></h3><p><b>Bears, 26-0:</b> So the Bucs think they can win without passing? That’s what they did last week, when Baker Mayfield went 0-for-3 in a shutout victory over the Falcons — never mind the monsoon. Let’s see if the Bucs can win without SCORING. Didn’t work for the Falcons, did it? <b>Season</b>: 3-5.<br></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview Six' prosecutor asks judge to delay high-stakes hearing where feds could take the stand
entries.summary: <p>A prosecutor who's<b> </b>been<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>to testify<b> </b>about the tainted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case asked a judge<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>to<b> </b>delay<b> </b>the<b> </b>hearing<b> </b>by<b> </b>a<b> </b>week, citing<b> </b>the<b> </b>possibility<b> </b>that his interests<b> </b>"may not be aligned" with others called to the stand — a list that includes U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan<b> </b>asked<b> </b>U.S. District Judge April<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>to push the Nov. 16 hearing<b> </b>back to<b> </b>Nov. 23. </p><p>He did so in a five-page brief<b> </b>filed by his attorney, Shelly<b> </b>Kulwin. It said Kulwin will be out of town before Nov. 16, and he will need "several days"<b> </b>to meet with Hogan<b> </b>and prepare for the hearing.</p><p>Hogan also asked Perry to clarify how the hearing will move forward, questioning<b> </b>whether his attorney will be allowed to cross-examine witnesses.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"While AUSA Hogan is unaware of the position the government may take at the upcoming hearing or the possible testimony of any other [assistant U.S. attorney] (or the United States attorney), it is quite possible that the government's interests, as well as some of the other proposed witnesses' testimony, 'may not be aligned' with his," Kulwin wrote in the court filing.</p><p>Perry<b> </b>earlier this week<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>Boutros, Hogan<b> </b>and two other rank-and-file prosecutors<b> </b>to testify in her courtroom. She did so while grappling with allegations of prosecutorial misconduct, which doomed the case filed last year against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters.<b> </b></p><p>Perry has specifically said<b> </b>Boutros' statements about the case<b> </b>are "hard to credit" and<b> </b>"nearly unfathomable."</p><p>Boutros is also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" target="_blank" >being sued</a> by Douglas DePodesta, the former special agent in charge of the FBI in Chicago. His lawsuit alleges that Boutros chased political prosecutions at the behest of President Donald Trump. Then, after the "Broadview Six" case fell apart, Boutros allegedly blamed DePodesta, falsely, for its failure within the Justice Department. </p><p>DePodesta said he was forced to resign.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" >‘Broadview 6' case heats up again as ex-FBI boss sues, top federal prosecutor ordered to testify</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" target="_blank" >has previously denied</a> that politics drove charging decisions in his office. The Justice Department has declined to comment on the pending litigation.</p><p>The "Broadview Six" case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. Prosecutors alleged that a crowd pushed and damaged a federal agent’s SUV.</p><p>But from that crowd, only six people were charged with a conspiracy to impede the agent. Most of them were involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about selective prosecution.</p><p>The defendants<b> </b>were<b> </b>then-congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, then-Cook County Board candidate Catherine<b> </b>“Cat”<b> </b>Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt, musician<b> </b>Joselyn<b> </b>Walsh<b> </b>and<b> </b>Abughazaleh<b> </b>campaign<b> </b>worker<b> </b>Andre<b> </b>Martin.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
